analysis.investment_thesis: Devyani International is a QSR franchise operator with strong brands (KFC, Pizza Hut) but economics that have never reliably translated into net profits — the company has been loss-making in 7 of 9 years and carries INR 3,188 Cr in debt at a forward P/E of 127x. The Ind AS 116 lease accounting flatters EBITDA, hiding the true cost of occupancy.
key_strengths: Franchise rights to globally recognized brands (KFC, Pizza Hut) with strong consumer recall and repeat purchase behavior
Revenue CAGR of 19.3% over 9 years demonstrates scale-building capability; FY25 revenue reached INR 4,951 Cr
OCF has been consistently positive (INR 301–900 Cr range over 5 years), indicating genuine cash generation at the store level before lease and finance costs
key_risks: Net profit negative in 7 of 9 years — including FY24 and FY25 — despite impressive revenue growth; scale has not delivered the promised margin expansion
Debt load of INR 3,188 Cr with finance costs of INR 267 Cr in FY25 growing at 22.5% CAGR — the company is funding expansion with expensive debt while losing money
Forward P/E of 127x is purely faith-based; if inflation, competition from Jubilant/Restaurant Brands, or consumer slowdown materializes, there is no earnings support for the price
red_flags: EBITDA of INR 853 Cr in FY25 looks reasonable until you remember Ind AS 116 inflates this figure by adding back lease costs — the true operating economics are significantly weaker
Equity was negative as recently as FY20 (-INR 189 Cr), reflecting years of accumulated losses burning through capital
Debt has nearly tripled from INR 1,254 Cr (FY22) to INR 3,188 Cr (FY25) as store expansion accelerated — unit economics must justify this capital at scale, and so far they haven't
analysis.detailed_analysis:
QSR franchisees can be excellent businesses when unit economics are strong — Jubilant Foodworks (Domino's) proved this. But Devyani's persistent inability to generate net profits despite operating 1,000+ outlets across KFC and Pizza Hut suggests that either rents are too high, execution is weak, or the brands' India unit economics are structurally inferior. The OCF is positive, which means individual stores generate cash — but after lease obligations and interest, there is nothing left for equity holders.

Inverting the thesis: at 127x forward earnings, you need sustained profitable growth for a decade to justify the price. The QSR sector in India is increasingly competitive with Burger King, McDonald's, and aggressive regional chains. Menu inflation and food delivery platform commissions (Zomato, Swiggy) compress margins further. The promoter (RJ Corp) has historically been willing to use leverage aggressively, which in a rising rate environment increases the chance of a capital raise that dilutes shareholders. I see limited margin of safety here.
